background.definition: A corneal abrasion is a self-limited, superficial injury to the outermost epithelial layer of the eye (cornea). A corneal ulceration is a local ulceration or focal necrosis of corneal tissue usually due to infection. Ulceration is usually preceded by trauma or corneal abrasion. Cornea ulcer is often referred to as microbial keratitis or infectious keratitis, as most cases have an infectious etiology.

list.listitem: A corneal abrasion is the most common eye injury in children presenting to emergency departments.
A corneal abrasion is the most common perioperative eye injury due to lagophthalmos (the inability to close eyelids and lubricate the eyes) during general anesthesia.
The most common causes of corneal abrasions are foreign bodies (particles, eyelashes, etc) and direct trauma (eg, from a fingernail).
Most corneal abrasions are infected and most infections are bacterial. The most common bacteria are Staphylococcus species and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Much less commonly, fungus may be the cause.
A common cause of corneal ulceration is a corneal abrasion that becomes infected.
A common cause of microbial keratitis is overnight wearing of silicone hydrogel contact lenses.

In one study of corneal ulcers children in children, contact lens wear was the most common reason for microbial keratitis, especially used in the setting of orthokeratology (using contact lenses to reshape the cornea).

Other causes of corneal ulceration include the use of extended-wear contact lenses, fungal infection due to overuse of steroid-containing ophthalmic drops, and disorders resulting in dry eyes (Sjogren's syndrome, Bell's palsy).
Half of patients with recurrent corneal erosions (RCE) have an epithelial basement membrane dystrophy (EBMD).
A corneal abrasion is caused by a mechanical disruption of outermost, anterior layer of the cornea.
Infection of the corneal defect often results in ulceration of the cornea and the formation of a corneal infiltrate of white blood cells.

list.listitem: There are no studies specifically examining the various components of the history or physical examination in either corneal abrasions or ulcers.

A typical presentation of corneal abrasion includes history of recent ocular trauma (eg, direct trauma, such as a scratch with a fingernail or foreign body, or dust blown into eye) followed by ocular pain or discomfort. Associated symptoms may include foreign body sensation, photophobia, tearing, burning, itching, blepharospasm, blurred vision, or headache.

Physical examination may reveal conjunctival redness, eyelid swelling, foreign body, and positive fluorescein staining (corneal defects appear yellow or green after application of fluorescein stain and examination with a cobalt blue light source).
Application of a topical ophthalmologic anesthetic (proparacaine or tetracaine) may facilitate an adequate examination if significant pain and/or blepharospasm are present.

The typical presentation of corneal ulcer includes moderate-to-severe pain, foreign body sensation, conjunctival redness and discharge, and blurred vision. There is often a history of preceding corneal trauma (abrasion). Use of extended-wear contact lenses is an important historical factor.

Slit-lamp examination reveals corneal infiltration (white blood cells in the anterior chamber) and a corneal epithelial defect that stains with fluorescein. Pus in the anterior chamber (hypopyon) can occur in severe cases.

A special case involves corneal ulceration due to the herpes simplex virus (HSV). It is associated with a vesicular dermatitis consistent with shingles over the distribution of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve. When found over the distribution of the nasociliary nerve (shingles on the tip of the nose, known as Hutchinson's sign), the risk for HSV infection of the cornea is high.

The use of fluorescein staining (abrasion appears yellow or green after application of fluorescein stain and examination with a cobalt blue light source, with or without a slit lamp) is useful in visualizing corneal abrasions and ulcers. The use of topical anesthetic can facilitate the examination if there is significant pain or blepharospasm.
There are no published data on test performance characteristics for examination with fluorescein staining.
Culture of eye discharge or corneal scraping is recommended in most cases of corneal ulceration, but not commonly performed in primary care practice.
Patients with corneal abrasion typically present with a history of recent ocular trauma, foreign body sensation, photophobia, tearing, blepharospasm, and blurred vision.
Use fluorescein stain and examine with a cobalt blue light source to confirm diagnosis (optionally aided by topical anesthetic to facilitate examination).
Patients with corneal ulcer typically present with progressive redness, moderate-to-severe pain, foreign body sensation, photophobia, and tearing.
Use fluorescein stain and examination with a slit-lamp to confirm the diagnosis of corneal ulcer. Culture of the discharge or scraping of the cornea is usually required.

Patching A and topical mydriatics B are not recommended for corneal abrasion.

While topical chloramphenicol may prevent corneal ulcerations in developing countries, low to very low certainty evidence from a systematic review found uncertainty in the efficacy and safety of topical antibiotic prophylaxis for preventing infection and improving healing time of corneal abrasions. Use combination fortified aminoglycoside/cephalosporin or fluoroquinolone monotherapy to treat corneal ulcers. Drops should be used every 15 to 30 minutes during the 1st day. B

No direct evidence is available from clinical trials regarding the efficacy of oral analgesics. However, given their wide availability and relative safety, consider oral analgesic medications for short-term pain control of corneal abrasion or ulcer.

Topical NSAIDs for corneal abrasions have unclear benefits based on conflicting evidence from systematic reviews. Based on a Cochrane review, topical NSAIDs for traumatic corneal abrasions are not supported by strong evidence in reducing pain and may lead to increased healthcare costs compared to oral analgesics. Another systematic review evaluating 31 RCTs and 2 cohort studies involving 4,167 patients with corneal abrasions found strong evidence that topical NSAIDs significantly improve pain at 24 and 48 hours, but do not affect healing time or adverse events. There are no good quality data measuring the effect of topical NSAIDs on earlier return to work.

Although commonly used, the short term use (≤72 hours) of topical anesthetics for corneal abrasion does not affect pain or healing rates; there are few safety data on the use of topical anesthetics. An emergency medicine guideline suggests that topical anesthetics may be safe and effective for slitlamp-verified simple corneal abrasions in relieving pain, but evidence for patient satisfaction is mixed. Use should be limited to 24 hours. This is based on a meta-analysis of two RCTs with 140 patients finding no difference in pain scores, corneal healing, or persistent symptoms.

The efficacy and safety of topical antibiotic prophylaxis for preventing infection and improving healing time of corneal abrasions are uncertain, based on low to very low certainty evidence from a Cochrane review of 2 RCTs enrolling 527 patients. However, studies in developing countries suggest that topical chloramphenicol begun within 18 hours of injury may prevent corneal ulcerations as a complication of corneal abrasions.

Standard treatment for corneal ulcerations includes the installation of antibacterial drops every 15 minutes to 30 minutes during the 1st day of treatment. Combination therapy with a fortified aminoglycoside and a fortified cephalosporin (tobramycin 1.3% and cefazolin 5%) or monotherapy with a fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin) may be equally effective.
Moxifloxacin (0.5% or 1.0%) ofloxacin (0.3%) and fortified tobramycin (1.33%)/cefazolin (5%) appear equally effective in the treatment of corneal ulcers.
Topical steroids (methylprednisolone) for corneal ulcers do not improve visual outcomes at 3 months.
Topical 5% natamycin is used to treat fungal keratitis. Topical and oral acyclovir are used to treat herpetic keratitis.
The American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) recommends systemic treatment of gonococcal keratitis and avoiding topical corticosteroids until bacterial keratitis has been controlled.

For patients with bacterial keratitis, povidone-iodine 1.25% was found to be similarly effective to neomycin-polymyxin B-gramicidine or ciprofloxacin 0.3% in a randomized trial, and is an option in under-resourced settings.

Do not treat corneal abrasion with eye patching as it does not appear to improve healing rates, reduce pain, or improve activities of daily living. It also leads to temporary loss of binocular vision.
It is a common practice to irrigate the eye to remove debris. If irrigating, use gently warmed saline solution.
Discontinue contact lens wear while corneal abrasion or ulceration is present.
A case series reported favorable results with platelet rich plasma for dorman corneal ulcers associated with surgery. However, there was no control group.
There is no good evidence that outlines the indications for, nor timing of, referral to an ophthalmologist.

Experts recommend referral for nonhealing abrasions, worsening pain, large abrasions, or a foreign body that is not easily removed. Experts also recommend that most cases of corneal ulcer be referred to an ophthalmologist.
Patients with HSV (shingles) involving the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve should be referred to an ophthalmologist for monitoring and immediate treatment of any eye involvement.
Experts recommend that patients with RCE be reffered to an ophthalmologist.
More than 90% of uncomplicated corneal abrasions will heal without treatment in 24 to 72 hours. B
Untreated corneal ulcerations can lead to corneal scarring and visual loss. C
Uncomplicated corneal abrasions heal without intervention or complications.

In 1 study, two thirds of corneal abrasions were healed 24 hours after injury, more than 80% were healed in 48 hours, and 90% were healed after 72 hours. In another study, more than 85% of patients had healed corneas 24 hours after the injury.
Untreated corneal ulcers can lead to corneal scarring and loss of vision.

One in 4 patients with corneal abrasions due to trauma by fingernail will report recurrent eye symptoms (photophobia, tearing, foreign body sensation, eye discomfort, or pain on awakening) for up to 3 months after the initial injury.
There are no data on long-term outcomes on clinically important measures such as change in visual acuity after corneal abrasions.
Corneal ulcers tend to heal with scar tissue, resulting in clouding of the cornea and decreased visual acuity.
In patients with fungal keratitis treated with 5% natamycin, infection with Aspergillus is associated with treatment failure.
One in 150 patients with a traumatic corneal abrasion will develop recurrent corneal erosions (RCE).
It is usual practice is to reevaluate the cornea 24 hours after injury and then every 24 to 72 hours until healed.

The diagnosis and management of corneal abrasions and ulcerations in children are the same as that in adults. There are no data reporting differences in diagnosis and treatment strategies between adults and children.
